# Diagnosing the 2004 Volvo XC90 Vacuum Assist Pump Loop

The symptom you are describingâa vacuum assist pump cycling continuously rather than just during cold startâis a classic failure mode in the 2004 Volvo XC90 T6 platform, specifically involving the electronic vacuum control unit (EVPU) or its associated piping. When the engine is cold, the ECU commands the EVPU to run briefly to build vacuum for the brake booster. Once warm, the system relies on manifold vacuum; the pump should disengage. If it activates periodically while driving or when stepping on the brake pedal, the control logic has detected a loss of vacuum and is attempting to compensate by running the pump indefinitely.

You have already performed the standard mechanical isolation steps: replacing the booster, master cylinder, intake gaskets, and throttle body gasket. You also confirmed the one-way valve at the turbo cooling pipe is functioning correctly. These are solid diagnostics that rule out common air leaks in the primary path. The persistence of the issue after replacing the vacuum ejector suggests the fault lies within the control signal or a secondary leak path that the ECU cannot compensate for without engaging the pump.

The fact that the pump engages when you turn the key to the second position (ignition on, engine off) and touch the brake is a critical diagnostic clue. In this state, the engine is not running, so there is zero manifold vacuum available. The system expects the EVPU to be off because it cannot build vacuum without an engine. However, if you apply pressure to the brake pedal in this state, the master cylinder will mechanically load against the booster diaphragm. If there is any air ingress anywhere in the line between the booster and the EVPU, the pressure differential collapses instantly. The ECU interprets this drop as "no vacuum" and commands the pump to run to restore it.

This behavior strongly points to a leak in the high-vacuum section of the plumbing or a faulty internal seal within the master cylinder itself that allows air to bypass the check valve, even if external gaskets are sound. While you mentioned checking the O-ring at the firewall, ensure you inspected the vacuum port on the master cylinder body for internal cracking or corrosion. Volvo master cylinders from this era can develop hairline fractures in the aluminum casting near the vacuum port base, which is invisible externally but catastrophic for vacuum integrity.

Another potential culprit is the check valve located inside the brake booster itself. Even if the booster unit was replaced with an "OEM quality" part, these units are notorious for having defective one-way valves that allow air to bleed backward from the booster into the EVPU line during pedal release. If air bleeds back when you lift your foot, the pressure drops below atmospheric relative to the pump outlet, tricking the ECU into thinking vacuum is lost.

Regarding the turbo cooling pipe connection you inspected: that specific T-connector acts as a secondary draw for vacuum to cool the turbocharger. If the valve on this line is stuck or if there is a micro-leak downstream of that valve (perhaps in the intake manifold runner near the turbo), it could create a significant enough load that the pump cannot maintain pressure without cycling. However, given your test where the pump runs even with no brake input while the car is stationary, a massive leak seems unlikely unless the EVPU itself is failing to shut off due to an electrical short or a faulty internal pressure sensor.

Before considering expensive electronic replacements, perform a "smoke test" on the entire vacuum train from the EVPU outlet to the booster inlet. You noted a weird smell in the cabin that makes your nose tingle; this is likely ozone or burnt rubber escaping through a hairline crack near the firewall or within the HVAC ducting that coincides with pump activation. Locating and sealing this leak while the system is under load will confirm if the cycling is purely mechanical or electrical. If the smoke test reveals no leaks, the EVPU module itself may have an internal pressure sensor that is stuck reading low, requiring a direct swap rather than further troubleshooting.
